question.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of $y = f(x)$ at $x=1$ is given by $f'(1).$

We will calculate $f'(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

\[
y = \sin{u}, \qquad u = \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right).
\]

Differentiating gives
\[
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = \cos{u}, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = \pi (2x + 2).
\]

We now apply the chain rule, and get

\begin{align*}
f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\\[5pt]

&=\cos u \cdot \pi (2x+2)\\[5pt]

&=\pi (2x+2)\cos u\\[5pt]

&=\pi (2x+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(x^{2} +2x - 2\right) \right).
\end{align*}

Evaluating at $x=1,$ we find

\begin{align}
f'(1) & =\pi (2\cdot1+2)\cos \left(  \pi \left(1^{2} +2\cdot1 - 2\right) \right) \\[3pt]

& =4\pi \cos(\pi) \\[3pt]
&= 4\pi \cdot (-1) \\[3pt]
&= -4\pi
\end{align}

Therefore, the slope $m$ of $y = f(x)$ at $x = 1$ is 
\[
m = f'(1) = \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{-4\pi}.
\]

knowledge_point.title: Differentiating a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
